c.tagline: Ottoman old town split by an emerald river and a leaping stone bridge.

taxi.fareNote: Uber and other ride-hailing apps do not operate in Mostar. Use local taxis; make sure the meter is running or agree a flat fare before setting off, especially from the airport or bus station.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that reaches police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Safe in town; uncleared landmines in some surrounding rural areas — stay on marked paths

hood_desc: The cobblestoned Ottoman core straddling the Neretva around Stari Most, the rebuilt 16th-century Old Bridge where divers leap into the river below; ringed by mosques, hammams and stone houses, it is where first-timers stay to be steps from every sight.

The copper-smiths' bazaar climbing the east bank in a tangle of cobbled lanes lined with stalls of handmade metalwork, rugs and souvenirs; the most atmospheric shopping in the city, busiest by day and quieter once the tour buses leave.
A quiet residential hillside just above the Old Town with guesthouses, gardens and views back over the minarets and river; a calmer base a short walk uphill from the crowds.

Mostar's modern west-bank heart around the Rondo roundabout and Španski Trg, with shopping centres, cafes, the bus and train stations and everyday city life; convenient and well-connected rather than picturesque.
A traditional east-bank neighbourhood of family homes, local eateries and orchards south of the Old Town; an authentic, budget-friendly area away from the tourist crush.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly from 6:00 AM to around 10:00 PM; there is no night service, so taxis fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Mostar has no metro or tram. The compact old-town core is best explored on foot; buses (operated by GIRO/Mostar Bus) cover the wider city and taxis handle everything else.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver (a few convertible marks per ride); there is no rechargeable transit card. Carry small change.

bus: Intercity coaches to Sarajevo, Dubrovnik, Split and Kotor
train: Mostar station on the Sarajevo–Čapljina–Ploče railway line (ŽFBH)

transit.m: Airport shuttle/local bus (limited, timed to some flights)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving ~10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Stari Most (Old Bridge)
Mostar's soaring 16th-century Ottoman bridge, rebuilt after the war, arcs 24 meters above the emerald Neretva while local divers plunge for tips.
Kujundžiluk (Old Bazaar)
Cobbled lanes of coppersmiths, carpet sellers, and café terraces tumble toward the Old Bridge, echoing Mostar's Ottoman market traditions since the 1500s.
Koski Mehmed-Pasha Mosque
Climb this 1618 mosque's slender minaret for the definitive postcard view of Stari Most framed by the Neretva canyon.
Kriva Ćuprija (Crooked Bridge)
A miniature single-arch Ottoman bridge over the Radobolja creek, said to be the trial run for its famous big brother nearby.
Blagaj Tekke
A 16th-century Dervish monastery clings to a cliff where the Buna River gushes fully formed from a cave mouth, an ethereal half-day trip.
Počitelj
This UNESCO-tentative fortified Ottoman village stacks stone houses, a mosque, and a citadel up a rocky amphitheater above the Neretva south of Mostar.
Kravice Waterfalls
Two dozen cascades pour over a 25-meter travertine crescent into a swimmable jade lagoon, Herzegovina's answer to a miniature Niagara.
Muslibegović House
An exquisitely preserved Ottoman nobleman's residence from the 18th century welcomes visitors to its carved interiors and rose-scented courtyard.
Museum of Old Bridge and Tara Tower
Inside the bridge's stout guard tower, exhibits and archaeological digs recount Stari Most's construction, wartime destruction, and painstaking rebirth.
Bišćevića House (Turkish House)
Perched dramatically over the Neretva, this 17th-century Ottoman home displays original divans, copperware, and a serene courtyard above the water.

intl.to: Ploče (Croatia) - seasonal Friday to Sunday summer service via Čapljina

train.note: Mostar's station on Trg Ivana Krndelja shares a site with the eastern bus station, about a kilometre from the Old Bridge. Two trains a day each way work the Sarajevo-Čapljina line through Mostar, taking roughly two hours to Sarajevo through the Neretva gorge - one of the finest short rail rides in the Balkans - with an early morning and an afternoon departure in each direction. ŽFBH's online ticket sales have been suspended for technical reasons, so buy at the counter in cash (about 11 KM to Sarajevo) at least a few minutes before departure. In summer the service is extended down to Ploče on the Croatian coast from Friday to Sunday, with passport checks at the border.

intl.to: Podgorica & Kotor (Montenegro), Belgrade (Serbia) - regional coaches from the eastern station

bus.note: Mostar has two bus stations reflecting the city's divide: the main eastern one at Trg Ivana Krndelja next to the railway station, open 07:00-20:00, and Mostar Zapad on Vukovarska, used mainly by Croat-run carriers - check which one your ticket names. Sarajevo takes about 2.5-3 hours, Split around 3.5-4, Dubrovnik 3-4 and Zagreb most of a day; Jajce and Podgorica are also served. Counter sales are cash in convertible marks or euros, while FlixBus and the regional booking sites let you pay online. Crossing into Croatia is now a Schengen external border, so keep your passport handy and expect queues at Doljani or Metković in summer.

ferry.note: Mostar lies on the Neretva about 60 km inland and the river is not navigable by passenger craft, so there are no boat services; the nearest ferry ports are Ploče and Split in Croatia, from where Jadrolinija sails to the Dalmatian islands and Ancona in Italy.

half.name: Medjugorje
half.blurb: A Catholic pilgrimage town where visions of the Virgin Mary were reported in 1981, now drawing millions of visitors yearly.

full.name: Sarajevo
full.blurb: The national capital, where Ottoman-era Baščaršija bazaar streets meet Austro-Hungarian architecture and wartime history.

full.name: Dubrovnik
full.blurb: A walled Adriatic coastal city with limestone streets and sea-facing ramparts, reached by crossing the Croatian border.
